client: I've been feeling completely stretched thin lately, like no matter what I do, I'm failing somewhere. I work these long shifts as a nurse, and then I come home to two little kids who need everything from me, and my partner is deployed so there's no one to share any of it with. I honestly don't know if talking about it is going to change the fact that I still have to go back and do it all again tomorrow.
therapist:
What you're carrying right now is genuinely enormous — holding life-and-death responsibility at work, then coming home to be the sole anchor for your kids, all while missing your partner and grieving that shared support. It makes complete sense that you'd wonder what talking can actually *do* when the weight doesn't go anywhere overnight, and I want to honor that honesty rather than brush past it. 

I'm not here to promise this changes tomorrow's shift or bedtime routine, but I am curious — in the middle of all that stretching, what does "failing" actually look like to you, and whose voice does it sound like?

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because I don't think anyone's ever asked it that way before. When I picture failing, it's like... a kid crying and me just standing there empty, or making a wrong call at work and someone not making it home. And honestly, the voice sounds like mine, but it's also a little bit my partner's, which is the part that really gets me, because they're not even here to actually say any of those things.
therapist: There's something really painful in what you just noticed — that the harshest critic in your head has borrowed your partner's voice, someone you love and miss, and is using it against you in moments when you're already running on empty. It's worth sitting with the fact that you *don't* just stand there empty — you showed up for that shift, you came home, you're here right now trying to understand yourself better, which is the opposite of the failure you're picturing. I'm wondering, if your partner were actually here and saw the full picture of what you're managing, do you think they'd truly be saying what that voice tells you?

client: I want to say no, they wouldn't say that, but honestly I'm not sure anymore. We ended things on such a bad note, and some of what they said at the end was really harsh, so part of me thinks maybe that voice is just... accurate. It's hard to separate what they actually believed about me from what was just said in anger.
therapist: That distinction you're trying to make — between what was said in a heated, painful moment versus what someone truly believes about you — is one of the most difficult and important things to untangle, and the fact that you're even questioning it rather than just accepting that voice as truth shows real insight. Words said in anger are often more about the pain of the person saying them than an accurate verdict on who you are, but I understand why they'd stick, especially when you're exhausted and your partner isn't here to give you any other data. What do you remember about who you were in that relationship *before* things got hard — is there another version of how they saw you that also lives in your memory?

client: I mean... yeah, there was a time when they used to call me their "steady one," like I was this anchor for them when things got chaotic in their life. But it's hard to hold onto that right now because it feels so far away, almost like it happened to different people. And honestly, part of me wonders if even that was real, or if I was just useful to them at the time and they eventually saw through to what I actually am.
therapist: That word "steady" is so significant, because it's actually what you're still doing right now — holding everything together for your kids, your patients, yourself — even while you're quietly wondering if any of it counts. The fear that you were only ever "useful" rather than truly valued is a painful thought, but I want to gently point out that it's a thought, not a fact, and it seems to show up most loudly when you're depleted and don't have your partner's present-day voice to counter it. I'm curious — if a close friend described themselves the way you just described yourself, as someone who might have just been "seen through," what would you want them to consider that they might be missing?

client: I'd probably tell a friend that they're being too hard on themselves, that one relationship not working out doesn't mean they were never really loved. But when I try to turn that around on myself, it just... doesn't land the same way. It feels like I'm just saying the words without actually believing them, like there's this wall between the logic and whatever I actually feel inside.
therapist: What you're describing — knowing the right words but feeling locked out of actually *believing* them — is one of the most common and frustrating experiences people bring to this kind of work, and it doesn't mean you're doing it wrong. That wall isn't a sign that the compassion isn't true; it's often a sign that the wound is deeper than logic can reach on its own, and that it needs something more than just reframing to slowly let the warmth in. I'm wondering, is there a moment — even a small one, recent or distant — where you felt something that didn't have to be argued into you, something that just felt real?

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my first instinct is to say no, nothing feels real anymore. But there was this one moment a few weeks ago when my neighbor's dog ran up to me on the street and just... was so happy to see me, tail going crazy, and for like thirty seconds I wasn't thinking about anything heavy. I don't know if that counts, or if it's kind of pathetic that a dog is the best example I can come up with.
therapist: It absolutely counts, and there's nothing pathetic about it — that dog didn't care about your shifts or your relationship or any of the weight you're carrying, it just responded to *you*, and something in you was able to receive that for thirty seconds without the wall getting in the way. That's actually really important information, because it tells us the capacity for feeling something real and good isn't gone, it's just been buried under exhaustion and grief and that relentless inner critic. I'm curious what it would mean for you to treat that moment not as a small or embarrassing exception, but as evidence of something that's still alive in you?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to hold onto that idea, like maybe it does mean something. But then there's this other voice that jumps in and says it was just a dog, it doesn't count as a real connection, and I'm grasping at straws if I think one random moment in a parking lot says anything meaningful about me. I guess I'm scared that if I let myself believe the capacity is still there, and then nothing actually changes, that's going to hurt a lot more than just staying numb.
therapist: What you just named is so honest and so human — that staying numb can feel like the safer bet, because hope has a cost, and you've already been paying so much. But I want to reflect something back: that voice that says "it was just a dog, it doesn't count" is the same voice that's been calling you a failure, borrowing your partner's harshest words — and we've already started to question whether that voice is a reliable narrator. The fear of hoping and being disappointed is real and worth taking seriously, but I'm wondering if numbness is actually protecting you right now, or if it's also quietly costing you something?

client: I hate that you're right about that voice, because it means I can't just dismiss what you're saying. But when you ask what numbness is costing me... I don't know, it feels like if I actually let myself grieve losing him properly, I'm admitting that that little corner of my life where I felt unconditionally loved is just gone now. And that's terrifying in a way I don't really have words for.
therapist: What you just said took real courage — naming that grief isn't just about losing a relationship, it's about losing the one place where you felt loved without having to earn it, without performing or holding everything together. That kind of loss deserves to be grieved properly, and the terror you're feeling makes complete sense, because that corner of your life mattered deeply. I want to sit with you in that for a moment before we try to do anything with it — can you tell me a little more about what that feeling of being unconditionally loved actually felt like when it was there?

client: It felt like... I don't know, like I could just exist without constantly checking whether I was too much or not enough. Like I didn't have to manage how I came across or worry that one wrong thing would make them pull away. I haven't felt that in so long that I'm honestly not sure I'd even recognize it anymore if it showed up again.
therapist: What you just described — that feeling of being able to simply *exist* without auditing yourself — is one of the most fundamental human needs there is, and it's quietly heartbreaking that it's felt so absent for so long that it's become almost unrecognizable to you. I want to gently point out that you just described it with real clarity and tenderness, which suggests some part of you still knows exactly what it feels like, even if it feels out of reach right now. I'm wondering, when you think about that quality — being able to exist without managing yourself — do you ever catch any glimpses of it, even briefly, maybe in unexpected places like a certain moment with your kids, or somewhere else in your life?

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my first instinct is to say no, not really. But actually... sometimes when I'm driving my kids to school in the morning and they're just chatting in the back seat about something completely random, I notice I'm just kind of there, listening, not thinking about whether I'm being a good enough parent in that moment. It's small, and it goes away fast, but yeah, I guess that's something.
therapist: That moment in the car is not small — that *is* the thing you said you couldn't recognize anymore, and it's happening between you and your kids, which means it didn't disappear when that relationship ended, it just moved. There's something really meaningful in the fact that it shows up when you're not trying, when you're just present and they're just being themselves and for a moment nobody needs anything to be different. I'm curious what it would feel like to start treating those moments not as accidents that go away too fast, but as proof that the capacity to simply exist — without checking yourself — is still yours?
